top.title: Scientists discover signs of a hidden extinction crisis deep beneath the ocean
top.summary: The deep sea has long been considered a safe haven for marine life, but new genetic research suggests a hidden biodiversity crisis may be unfolding far beneath the waves. Scientists analyzing more than a decade of genetic data from five species of deep-sea fish and shrimp in the Gulf discovered troubling signs of extinction risk in every species examined.

top.title: For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work
top.summary: A major new study challenges a long-standing assumption about how the brain works, revealing that most neurons are versatile multitaskers rather than highly specialized workers. By analyzing recordings from 43 regions of the mouse brain, researchers discovered that although some neurons are dedicated to specific functions, most respond to a wide variety of information in remarkably distinct ways.

top.title: Runaway pulsar escapes the remnant of its own supernova
top.summary: A team of astronomers has spotted a rare example of a pulsar that has escaped the cloud of debris left by the supernova explosion in which it formed. Led by Rohit Dokara, formerly at the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy, the team made the discovery by chance, adding to just a handful of similar known cases.

top.title: Protein redesign boosts DNA insertion activity and reveals how molecular machinery selects targets
top.summary: Genome engineering is exciting, given its vast potential to treat and even cure diseases, but it is still a largely uncharted biomedical innovation. Scientists at St. Jude Children's Research Hospital recently uncovered the mechanisms involved in precisely integrating DNA into a target genomic location using CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs).

top.title: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time

more.title: Deep beneath Australia, hidden caves could unlock the secrets of alien worlds

These subtle landscape features are created as deeply buried cave systems slowly collapse upward over millions of years. The discovery could help researchers locate unexplored caves containing ancient environmental records and unusual life forms.

more.title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
more.summary: A famous 345-million-year-old fossil has turned out to be something entirely different from what scientists believed for decades. Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.

more.title: Some miniature Cas12m proteins can cut DNA after all
more.summary: An international research group led by graduate student Hayato Morinaga, Assistant Professor Satoshi N. Omura and Professor Osamu Nureki from the University of Tokyo has demonstrated for the first time that some Cas12m proteins do have an active state capable of cutting, or "cleaving," DNA. The team also clarified the structural differences between the active and inactive variations.

more.title: Digital access to early music
more.summary: What may look to modern readers like a form of secret code in fact opens the door to a fascinating world of historical music: German lute tablature. Developed specifically for the Renaissance lute, this rich notational tradition preserves dances, songs and other musical works that were immensely popular some 500 years ago.

more.title: Why molecular cage catalysts show enormous differences in performance
more.summary: Chemistry researchers have developed a new way to identify and understand highly effective artificial enzyme-like catalysts using powerful "molecular cages" that mimic the behavior of nature's enzymes. These tiny, hollow molecular structures act like miniature reaction chambers to trap molecules and accelerate chemical reactions.

more.title: DESTINY model tracks molecular chemistry on uneven, ice-covered grains in interstellar space
more.summary: Interstellar space is the scene of active chemical processes: molecules form there in the gas, but also on the surface of tiny dust grains covered in ice. To better represent what happens on these surfaces, astrophysicists at the University of Liège are proposing a deterministic approach based on Markov chains with absorbing states, a mathematical tool that had not yet been utilized in astrochemistry.

more.title: God-faced rings may have identified Mesoamerica's long-distance merchants
more.summary: Over 1,000 years ago, a Mesoamerican may have been traveling through foreign lands. Upon arriving at his destination, he held up his hand, adorned with a ring showing the face of a god, but what was this ring's purpose?

more.title: Global maritime trade set for zero growth in 2026: UN
more.summary: Global maritime trade—which carries more than 80% of the world's goods—is set to stagnate in 2026 due to shipping disruptions and trade uncertainties arising from the war in the Middle East, the United Nations said Thursday.

more.title: Do all groups drift toward rule by the few? Not when time is on their side
more.summary: For more than a century, a bleak idea has hung over the ideal of democracy: Given enough time, every group ends up ruled by a few. The idea, known as the iron law of oligarchy, was first proposed by the sociologist Robert Michels in the early 1900s.

more.title: Learning facts out of interest may take less mental effort than learning them for money
more.summary: When completing tasks or acquiring information, humans can be driven by intrinsic and extrinsic motivations. The term intrinsic motivation entails doing something because it is interesting to us or we find it enjoyable, while extrinsic motivation means doing it to obtain a reward, such as money, praise or a good grade.

more.title: Two mechanisms of amino acid transport in a rare disease-associated protein revealed
more.summary: Cells must constantly exchange amino acids with their environment to make proteins and support numerous bodily processes. To do this, they have specialized transporters located in their membranes.

more.title: Early Stone Age rock carvings in Scandinavia may have been signposts for hunting grounds
more.summary: Between roughly 9,000 and 4,000 B.C., artists in ancient Scandinavia painstakingly carved large, sometimes life-size images of elk, reindeer, bears and other creatures into rock faces teetering on the edge of fjords, rivers and lakes. But their meaning has long been debated.
